description: A slow-growing, thorny, deciduous tree 8-15 m tall with trifoliate aromatic leaves, fragrant greenish-white flowers and round woody-shelled fruits whose sweet-sticky orange pulp contains many seeds.
cultural_significance: Sacred to Lord Shiva: trifoliate bilva leaves are offered in Shiva worship, especially on Mahashivaratri, and the tree is planted in temple precincts. Called Shriphala ('fruit of prosperity'). Prominent in the Samhitas, Puranas and Nighantus.
habitat: Dry deciduous forests and plains of the Indian subcontinent; planted near temples and in home gardens; tolerates poor, rocky and saline soils.

uses.title: Diarrhoea and dysentery
uses.detail: The unripe or dried fruit pulp is described as Grahi (absorbent) and is a classical remedy for chronic diarrhoea and dysentery.

uses.title: Constipation and gut health
uses.detail: The ripe fruit pulp is traditionally taken as a mild laxative and a digestive cooling drink (sherbet) in summer.

uses.title: Part of Dashamoola
uses.detail: The root bark is one of the ten roots of Dashamoola, used in fever, respiratory and Vata disorders.

uses.title: Leaf paste for swelling and eye care
uses.detail: Leaf juice and paste are traditionally used externally for swelling and in some eye conditions.

uses.title: Blood sugar research
uses.detail: Leaf extracts show glucose-lowering effects in animal studies; human evidence is limited.

classical_refs: Charaka Samhita - bilva is among the commonly used Mulini and Dashamoola herbs

preparations.name: Bael sherbet
preparations.method: Scoop ripe pulp, mash with water and strain; sweeten with jaggery or sugar.
preparations.note: Cooling summer drink; the ripe fruit is mildly laxative.

preparations.name: Dried fruit powder
preparations.method: Slice unripe fruit, sun-dry and powder; take with water or buttermilk.

preparations.name: Leaf juice or paste
preparations.method: Crush fresh leaves for juice or a paste.
preparations.note: Traditional household use; check with a practitioner.

preparations.name: Bilvadi churna
preparations.method: Classical powder with dried bael fruit and other digestive herbs.

precautions: May lower blood sugar, so people on diabetes medicines should consult a doctor. Excess intake of the ripe fruit may cause bloating or loose stools, while the unripe fruit is constipating. The root and bark are used with care in pregnancy. The tree has sharp thorns; allergy to Rutaceae plants is possible.

cultivation.climate: Tropical to subtropical; tolerates heat and mild frost
cultivation.soil: Well-drained loam; tolerates poor, rocky or saline soil
cultivation.harvest: Fruits ripen from about March to May after nearly a year on the tree

conservation_status: Near Threatened (IUCN) in parts of its range due to over-exploitation; widely planted.
fun_fact: Bael leaves always grow in groups of three, which Shiva devotees associate with the god's trident and three eyes.
